title: Why China Is the Bogeyman Data Center Enthusiasts Just Can't Quit
gist: As US public opposition to data centers hits 75% and both parties turn against the infrastructure ahead of the midterms, tech boosters and Trump-aligned figures are pushing a thinly-evidenced narrative that Chinese influence operations — not genuine environmental and economic grievances — are driving the backlash.

themes.theme: Rising public and political backlash against data centers

insights.claim: As many as 75 percent of Americans now say they would oppose a data center being built in their area, up from 42 percent a year earlier, indicating a rapid escalation in public opposition to data center construction.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A jump from 42% to 75% opposition in a year is a fast-moving local-permitting and siting risk for any company planning new US data center capacity, independent of federal policy support.
insights.quote: as many as 75 percent of Americans now say they would oppose a data center being built in their area, up from 42 percent last year
insights.locator: It’s been a rough summer for data center boosters

insights.claim: Politicians from both parties who previously supported data center development, including Texas governor Greg Abbott and Pennsylvania governor Josh Shapiro, are now shifting toward a harder line against data centers as the midterms approach.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Bipartisan political retreat from data center advocacy in swing/growth states raises the odds of new state-level restrictions or permitting friction regardless of federal support under Trump.
insights.quote: Politicians from both parties who were previously advocates, like Texas governor Greg Abbott and Pennsylvania governor Josh Shapiro, are now switching up
insights.locator: Politicians from both parties who were previously advocates

insights.claim: President Trump has voiced vigorous support for data center construction even as some Republicans in his own party turn against the issue ahead of the midterms.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A split within the Republican coalition between the White House's pro-buildout stance and local politicians reading anti-data-center polling signals policy uncertainty at the state level even where federal posture stays supportive.
insights.locator: But while some Republicans are turning tail on the issue

insights.claim: In late August, X said it had identified 200 accounts linked to China spreading anti-data-center talking points on the platform, a finding that generated a wave of alarmist headlines, including Axios describing China as 'secretly fueling America's data center rage.'
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A single platform's account-takedown report became the evidentiary basis for a widely amplified political narrative, illustrating how thin source material can scale into a dominant media storyline.
insights.quote: China is secretly fueling America's data center rage
insights.locator: In late August, X announced that it had identified 200 accounts

insights.claim: President Trump amplified the China-blame narrative directly, posting on Truth Social that 'China could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement' just days after X's report, while defending data center construction under the phrase 'let Data Reign.'
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Presidential-level amplification of the China-blame framing makes it a durable talking point that could shape federal policy responses (e.g., justifying platform crackdowns or trade measures) regardless of its evidentiary weakness.
insights.quote: China could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement

insights.claim: OpenAI banned a cluster of accounts in June that it said were linked to the Chinese government and were 'testing narratives against AI infrastructure,' feeding into the broader claim that Chinese influence operations are driving anti-data-center sentiment.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: OpenAI's own account ban is being cited as corroborating evidence for the China narrative, so its details matter for judging how much genuine foreign-influence risk exists around AI infrastructure sentiment.
insights.locator: In June, OpenAI banned a cluster of users

insights.claim: OpenAI's own June report acknowledged that the flagged account cluster was simply exploiting pre-existing discontent about data centers rather than manufacturing the opposition from scratch, and X's broader bot-farm takedown found 200,000 total accounts, of which the 200 anti-data-center accounts were a small fraction that may overlap with OpenAI's flagged cluster based on shared hashtags, images, and a common local news article.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: The source's own admission that it found amplification of existing sentiment, not manufactured opposition, undercuts the stronger 'China caused the backlash' framing being used in political messaging.
insights.quote: In its own report from June, OpenAI acknowledged that the cluster of accounts it identified was simply exploiting existing discontent around data centers.
insights.locator: In its own report from June, OpenAI acknowledged

insights.claim: Social media analytics firm Graphika, which has tracked data center sentiment online since at least June, told the author that most of the opposition it has observed is homegrown, with still very little evidence of significant foreign intervention.
insights.speaker: Tyler Williams
insights.so_what: An independent analytics firm's consistent finding of homegrown opposition over multiple months is the strongest counter-evidence in the piece against the foreign-influence framing, useful for discounting China-blame headlines when assessing genuine data-center siting risk.
insights.locator: There’s still very little evidence of significant foreign intervention

insights.claim: Pro-data-center blogger Andy Masley, who is popular with tech boosters and has publicly requested insider evidence of Chinese intervention, says he has not received anything solid and suspects the China narrative is a 'convenient belief' for people who have adopted more right-wing framing.
insights.speaker: Andy Masley
insights.so_what: Skepticism from within the pro-data-center camp itself is a signal that the China narrative may be serving a political/rhetorical function rather than reflecting verified intelligence, relevant for discounting the framing in policy analysis.
insights.quote: It seems like a very convenient belief.
insights.locator: Masley has put out a public call for any insider information

insights.claim: WIRED's senior business editor and China specialist Louise Matsakis argues the episode reflects a basic misunderstanding of what real Chinese influence campaigns look like, and that panics blaming China for domestic backlash are less about China than about Americans finding it easier to scapegoat a foreign 'other' than examine their own grievances.
insights.speaker: Louise Matsakis
insights.so_what: This framing suggests investors should treat 'China influence' claims around US infrastructure backlash as a recurring rhetorical pattern rather than a reliable predictor of policy outcomes, and instead track the underlying local economic/environmental grievances directly.
insights.quote: Americans often find it easier to put the blame on a nebulous other, rather than to actually look at themselves.
insights.locator: “It is endlessly fascinating to me how China becomes a scapegoat,”

insights.claim: The China-blame narrative coexists uneasily with simultaneous complaints from Trump administration officials that Chinese firms are stealing American AI advances, since it is unclear why China would want to slow the same US AI infrastructure buildout its own AI models are allegedly benefiting from.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: This internal contradiction is a useful sanity check for evaluating any policy or media claim that ties Chinese strategy to opposing US AI infrastructure growth.

insights.claim: Meta is pushing to build out a robot workforce inside its data centers, a shift that could let the company cut costs on services like food and janitorial staff as automation reduces on-site technical jobs, according to WIRED colleague Paresh Dave's reporting.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: Data center automation reducing on-site headcount (including support-service jobs like cafeteria and janitorial staff) is a direct local-economic-impact channel that could feed the very public backlash the article discusses, independent of any foreign influence.
insights.quote: I was surprised to learn that some data centers have cafeterias, with full-on kitchen staff
insights.locator: My colleague Paresh Dave wrote an eye-opening piece

insights.claim: Utility company Entergy sought a restraining order against the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette after the paper published details, obtained via a public records request, of Entergy's data-center-related deal with Google, with Entergy claiming trade secrets were accidentally released and pursuing the mother who filed the original records request.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A utility attempting to suppress public disclosure of a data-center power deal via legal action against a newspaper and a private citizen is a direct transparency and legal-risk flashpoint tied to data center growth, worth monitoring in states with similar utility-hyperscaler deals.
insights.locator: An outrageous story is unfolding in Arkansas

insights.claim: The Financial Times reported that AI has contributed to high unemployment among college graduates in Texas, a state that hosts one of the largest concentrations of data centers under development.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A reported link between AI-driven job displacement and a major data-center hub state adds a concrete economic grievance that could sustain local political backlash independent of any foreign-influence narrative.
insights.locator: The Financial Times covers how AI has caused high unemployment

insights.claim: The Washington Post reported a massive new influx of state-level legislation on data centers is heading into the 2026-2027 legislative year.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A wave of incoming state legislation is the concrete regulatory catalyst to track for data center operators and their utility/investor partners, likely to include siting, tax, or power-allocation restrictions.
insights.locator: The Washington Post reports on a massive new influx
